subsubtopic: TABLING OF DOCUMENT SHAPING CANADA'S FUTURE TOGETHER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 32(2), I have the honour to table, in both official languages, copies of a document entitled Shaping Canada's Future Together.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to table the government's proposals to renew the Canadian federation. The proposals, entitled Shaping Canada's Future Together have one simple but nevertheless critical and crucial objective; to build a stronger and more prosperous Canada where all Canadians can feel at home. I believe that is an objective that is shared by all members of this House who believe in Canada.
Every generation of Canadians has had to redefine the terms of living together. Our generation now faces that same challenge. If we are wise and remain true to our traditions, we can transform challenge into opportunity. Our goal is not only a framework under which all Canadians can feel at home in this magnificent country, but one that better equips us to meet the challenges of the global economy in the 21st century and beyond. Because if we must provide Canadians with a valid constitution, we must also provide Canadians with a powerful and a growing economy. And one goes with the
other, and these two challenges have to be met by all members of this House.
Canada's needs are well known: aboriginal self-government; two Houses of Parliament that are truly democratic and progressively more responsive; recognition, in principle and in practice, of the distinctive character of Quebec; protection for the rights of all Canadians, particularly for minorities; a stronger Canadian economic union; bringing government closer to the people in framing national programs and in delivering programs and services to individual Canadians, to people; reducing wasteful overlap and duplication of government programs. There is not a member in this House who has not heard directly from his or her voters in regard to not only the overlap and the waste in government, but the perception that it is perhaps in some cases even more widespread than actually meets the eye. Of course, governments at all levels, not just Ottawa, must listen and lead and one that truly empowers people in exercising its powers.
Mr. Speaker, none of these changes is in any way contrary to the original concept of Confederation, now 125 years old. Rather, these changes add up to a renewal, now long overdue if the truth be known, of our Confederation.

Renewal is what Canadians everywhere seek for our country-not confrontation, not division, not rupture. Renewal of our values, of our institutions, of our working arrangements-renewal of the spirit of Confederation so that we can face the future more confidently together. Finally, renewal of our commitment to Canada and to the well-being of our fellow Canadians.
The proposals I am tabling today on behalf of the government will be referred to the Special Joint Committee on a Renewed Canada. These proposals are for discussion. That committee has five months to consult with Canadians. Its mandate is very broad. The process is open, not closed; it is inclusive, not exclusive.

Routine Proceedings

We seek improvements to our proposals and we expect changes. The joint committee will hold its first meeting tomorrow. The first witness before that joint committee will be the right hon. Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs, whose outstanding leadership in developing these proposals I know that all members from all parties will want to acknowledge with respect and gratitude.
Hear, hear.

Today, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to go into a detailed explanation of all of these proposals. They will be available to members of the House, to the media and eventually to all Canadians. Rather, I wish simply to outline them so as to convey to the people of Canada what lies behind the proposals, the spirit that motivates them and the objectives we had in mind in developing them.
In the Canadian constitutional tradition, there exists side by side protection for individual human rights and the rights of people as members of communities. The people of Canada cherish these rights as attributes of our common citizenship. They are defining characteristics of our Canadian identity. They capture in many ways the essence of what unites us.
Our proposals therefore seek to enhance both individual and collective rights. For example, we are proposing that the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms be amended to guarantee property rights among our basic rights in Canada.
Hear, hear.

We are also proposing more stringent limitations on the use of the so-called notwithstanding clause which enables legislatures to override many of our basic rights.
Of the various communities whose rights need and deserve protection, the aboriginal peoples of Canada have, in my judgment, a very important claim on our attention and the attention of all members. We have made a commitment to them that they will participate in the current constitutional discussions. We propose to entrench a continuing constitutional process for aboriginal matters. Consistent with these guarantees of process,
the time has come to break with our recent history in aboriginal constitutional matters which sadly, has largely been by any objective criteria, a history of failure.
We are proposing to entrench in the Constitution of Canada a general right to aboriginal self-government within the Canadian federation and subject to the Charter.
Hear, hear.

Our proposal would allow governments and aboriginal peoples 10 years to agree on the powers to be exercised, failing which they would be defined and enforced by the courts. In other words, the passage of time would work for and not against the aboriginal peoples of Canada. No aboriginal leader I know believes that self-government is by itself the remedy for the terrible deprivation and alienation that are so prevalent among so many aboriginal peoples. None underestimates the value of regaining the right to self-government and the responsibility that goes with it in providing an opportunity for First Nations' renewal.
That is what they ask, the right to get on with their own lives as members of aboriginal societies, the right to devise their own solutions to the terrible problems which over generations have come to afflict these societies, the right to work out their own place by themselves in Canada's future and the chance of a new lease on life.
I am proposing a deadline on the negotiation of the powers of aboriginal self-government because-I want everyone in Canada to understand this-I believe that we dare not wait another generation.
This is a matter of human dignity, of justice and fairness. We cannot repair the past, but we need not be condemned to relive it either. Let us altogether ensure that the future of the aboriginal peoples belongs to them and to their children in fairness, justice and equality of opportunity for all.

Mr. Speaker, about 285 million English-speaking people live on the North American continent. Surrounded by all these English-speakers is one piece of territory, Quebec, where some six million French-speaking people live and are a majority. They are determined to preserve and promote a vibrant French-speaking society in Quebec. They want to live their lives in French in a Canada that is both prosperous and fair. We must make certain that their capacity to do so is not inhibited, but is

enhanced by reform of our Constitution and renewal of our Confederation.
Constitutional reform must embrace Quebec's distinct society and we propose to do so, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear.

Ninety-three years before Confederation, not after, but before Confederation, the Parliament of Great Britain recognized the distinctiveness of Quebec. The Quebec Act established Quebec's right to preserve its religion and civil laws. Exactly 200 years ago, Mr. Speaker, the Constitution Act of 1791 continued those rights. The British North America Act of 1867 rejected conclusively the attempt in 1840 to submerge those rights in a unitary system and contained other provisions supporting the distinctive character of Quebec.
The modem world with its economic, social and population pressures has in some respects overtaken the old Constitution and bent it out of shape. It is not surprising then that of all the provinces, Quebec has for 30 years been the principal advocate of constitutional reform.
In 1982, the isolation of Quebec from the patriation of our Constitution was a powerful reminder to Quebecers of their minority status and vulnerability as a society in English-speaking North America. In spite of the compelling economic and social advantages to Quebec of participating in Confederation-and no serious person in Quebec doubts those advantages-Quebec will assume the risks and responsibilities as well as the rights of a new federal partnership only if Confederation guarantees her cultural security as a distinct French-speaking society in Canada on American soil.
Hear, hear.

Seven years ago, Mr. Speaker, I committed my government to securing the return of Quebec to the Canadian constitutional family. We have never wavered in that commitment and today, Mr. Speaker, I reaffirm our determination to succeed.
I am sure that Quebecers will see in today's proposals the possibility of achieving the fundamental reforms that Quebec needs to evolve as a distinct society within Canada and to be a secure, confident and equal partner
Routine Proceedings
in Confederation. I have no doubt that this can be accomplished to the enduring benefit of all Canadians.
With regard to the recognition of Quebec's distinct society, we are proposing that clause 2 of the Constitution, a Canada clause, affirm the special responsibility of Quebec to preserve and promote its distinct identity as a French-speaking society. We are also proposing that the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms be interpreted consistent with the preservation and promotion of Quebec as a distinct society within Canada. It must never be forgotten that Quebec is a distinct society, but always within a united Canada.
The affirmation of Quebec's distinctive character in the Canada Clause and the recognition of the distinct society in the Charter of Rights would be important and substantial amendments to our Constitution. They are essential safeguards for Quebec against the uncertainties of the future.
In our proposals relating to national institutions, distribution of powers and the economic union, Quebec will find the space and the freedom to evolve and to flourish as a distinct society in a more harmonious Confederation. Our proposals relating to the Senate contain additional protection for the French language and culture. And, Mr. Speaker, if collectively we find it desirable next spring to include in our plan any items that require unanimity, we will move forward with important amendments to the amending formula and additional changes to the Supreme Court of Canada to which we remain committed as a government.
The proposal to place labour market training under exclusive provincial jurisdiction is fundamental reassurance of the authority of Quebec and of the other provinces over matters related to education. The proposed entrenchment of immigration agreements such as that recently signed by the federal government and Quebec has long been regarded by Quebec as a vital element of her cultural security. Now we are proposing the negotiation and entrenchment of similar agreements on cultural matters with any province that so requests. We will define the roles of governments to reflect the particular circumstances of each province in cultural matters. The proposals for delegation of federal legislative power, as well as for administrative delegation in some fields-and the proposed rules on the use of the

Routine Proceedings
federal government's spending power-would create a far more flexible federalism than we have known, something many have advocated.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that we all know that the people of Canada are going to be looking carefully to see whether in proposing change and renewal for Canada we parliamentarians might seek to exempt ourselves. Well, we cannot and we must not. I am sure that we all realize that in the minds of the people of Canada no area of our national life is more in need of improvement than the Parliament of Canada itself.
I want to draw your attention to our proposals for reform of the House of Commons. Some may say these proposals breach long-standing parliamentary traditions. I would argue to the contrary, that these proposals are more faithful than some of our modem practices have been to the essence of parliamentary government and MP's prerogatives and individual freedoms. If we pursue proposals along these lines, we will have government much more responsive to the elected representatives of the people, and we will have members of Parliament much more responsive to the people who elected them in the first place.
We will then be closer to the British system of parliamentary government as it was originally meant to be. We will have a more vibrant and a more vital Canadian parliamentary democracy.
The people of Canada properly demand a renewed House of Commons and a reformed Senate. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that our Senate proposals are very much in line with the expectations of people across Canada, but I look forward to the views of the public and the recommendations of the parliamentary committee.
The Senate that we are proposing today would, for the first time, be directly elected by the people of Canada. An unelected body exercising legislative powers equal to the House of Commons is simply not compatible with democratic government.
The Senate should also be much more equitable in its representation than is the present chamber. Equity includes a range of possibilities, from weighted representation of member states, such as in Germany, to equal representation of provinces as advocated by the Canada West Foundation.
We propose an effective Senate. As a general rule, in order for a measure to become law, the approval by both the House of Commons and the reformed Senate should be necessary. And the Senate should have to approve key government appointments that affect the lives of Canadians. For example, under this plan in the future, nominees such as the Governor of the Bank of Canada would have to go before a reformed, elected Senate to explain his philosophy and obtain the approval of that body.
On legislation involving language and culture, special voting rules, a double linguistic majority will apply as proposed, Mr. Speaker, by the Alberta legislative committee in 1983, and by the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador in 1989.
On matters of particular national importance such as defence and international relations, the Senate would only have a suspensive veto.
Under our proposals, the House and the Senate would have somewhat different roles and responsibilities. We believe that good government demands that only the House of Commons be a confidence chamber, in order to prevent the kind of constitutional instability that parliamentary federal systems have known at other times and in other jurisdictions.
The Commons would likely become a chamber in which there was stricter adherence to the principle of representation by population, and the Senate in consequence, would provide more balanced and more equitable representation among the provinces. Both houses would have real power. Most important to Canadians, the Senate, like the House of Commons, would for the first time be accountable and responsible to the people of Canada.
I think, Mr. Speaker, there would not be much quarrel about it, that in the eyes of most people, for the first time the reformed Senate would have, as it is proposed today or perhaps as is modified by the parliamentary committee, democratic legitimacy.
Mr. Speaker, for some years Canadians have felt an increasing frustration with governments at all levels, and that is pretty obvious to all of us. Millions of Canadians sense they have lost power and influence over decisions that affect them, their families and the places they live. We must act to try and bring government closer to people. The reforms that we are proposing to the House of Commons and the Senate would greatly improve the

responsiveness of parliamentarians to the people who elect them in the first place.

But bringing government closer to the people also means sharing power and responsibility with provincial and municipal governments and with non-governmental organizations.
Matters such as labour market training, immigration and culture have important national dimensions for the Canadian economy and indeed for the Canadian identity. Our proposals would preserve the capacity of the federal Parliament to maintain the national interest and institutions in these matters. However, training, immigration and cultural policy affect some of the most sensitive areas of people's lives. Mr. Speaker, that is why we are proposing that provinces have control over training as they have over education.
Hear, hear.

That is why we propose to negotiate and entrench in the Constitution federal-provincial agreements on immigration, tailored to the particular needs, priorities and traditions of each province, from British Columbia to Newfoundland. That is also why we propose to negotiate and entrench in the Constitution similar agreements on cultural responsibilities with provincial governments that so request, while maintaining the federal Parliament's responsibility-and I say it clearly, Mr. Speaker, to avoid any misunderstanding-over key national institutions such as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the Canada Council.
That is also the spirit behind our proposal to recognize the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces in such areas as housing, forestry, municipal affairs and tourism, while maintaining our international responsibilities in these areas. That is the spirit behind our proposal to require the federal government to work with the provinces in introducing new Canada-wide shared cost programs in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction.
However, Mr. Speaker, financing would still be provided to a province which preferred to tailor its own
Routine Proceedings
program to its own needs, so long as it met the objectives of the new national program.
Mr. Speaker, I believe we all know that the need to bring government closer to the people-and to share and to decentralize power-has to be balanced with the requirement for a strong Canadian political and economic union.

To reinforce the bonds that must unite us and to strengthen our capacity to compete and prosper in the world, our proposals include several fundamental reforms to our economic union.
There are more interprovincial barriers to trade and commerce within Canada today than there are among nations of the European common market. These barriers in our internal market weaken the Canadian economy and impair our ability to compete in the world. That is why we are proposing that the Constitution be amended to prohibit government barriers to the mobility of people, goods, capital and services anywhere within Canada.
In law and in fact our economic growth is profoundly affected by the policies and actions of both the federal and provincial governments. Fundamental conflict between federal and provincial economic policies can be absolutely disastrous. Even working at cross purposes can diminish our prosperity. It is absurd that the 12 nations of the European common market are moving toward a state of economic co-ordination and harmonization superior in many ways to the Canadian economic union which has been together for 125 years. Obviously we must do better. We must equip this country with the means to act decisively to ensure the best we can our own prosperity.
That is why we are proposing to amend the Constitution to provide the Parliament of Canada with a new power to make laws for the efficient functioning of the economic union of Canada.
That is why we are making a number of proposals to formalize the co-ordination of federal and provincial economic and fiscal policies. Together it is these reforms that produce the strongest framework of economic union since Confederation.

September 24, 1991
Routine Proceedings
We propose as well a Canada clause which would be entrenched in the body of the Constitution, in section 2 of the Constitution Act. I hope and believe that all of our people will see reflected in that clause their own place in Canada, the common values and aspirations that unite us and our national characteristics, and our identity as we wish it to be.
We are a nation with an immense capacity for generosity and compromise, a capacity that has never mattered more than it matters today. Parochialism, small-mindedness, mistrust: these are always present in any society. These lesser attributes have had their day. It is now time for the fundamental qualities of generosity and compromise to dominate the process.
There are in all 28 proposals that the Government of Canada is putting forward today for consideration by the joint committee and discussion with the people of Canada.

Before presenting our plan for renewal in final form, we want to have the report of the Joint Committee, whose mandate extends until February. As I undertook to this House on May 15, "the government will be very open-minded to constructive amendments offered in the spirit of improving its proposals and broadening the consensus that Canadian unity needs and demands".
The government's proposals should be and will be examined on their merits. They must also be considered in light of their purpose, which is a more secure, united and prosperous Canada.

These proposals which are perfectible and which are going to a committee beginning hearing tomorrow will hopefully be examined in an objective and fair-minded manner, not by people searching for perfection because perfection can become the enemy of the good but for proposals that are good for Canada.
No one need lose. If the cause, the hopes and the aspirations of western Canada are advanced, that does not mean that that advancement means a loss for Quebec.
If French Canadians feel no more secure as a result of constitutional proposals and feel a greater attachment
and greater love for Canada, that does not mean that the rights of Canadians in English speaking Canada, say in the Atlantic region, will in any way be diminished.
Constitutional proposals fairly considered, actively debated, and generously contemplated can be what they should be: a win-win situation for all Canadians.
How are they to be considered? Each one of us across the country, each premier, each taxpayer, each parliamentarian, each of us, will have to establish, I suppose, his or her own sense of parameters and his or her own objective criteria. I think that these proposals must also be considered in light of our greatest obligation.
We have many obligations. You can enumerate them, you can count them, you can divide them and you can add them up, but our greatest obligation as Canadians and as parliamentarians sitting here today is to turn Canada over to our children and grandchildren unsullied, undiminished and as a great, prosperous, united nation. That is our fundamental obligation.
To do that will require compromise and compromise is not an indication of weakness. Honourable compromise in Canada has always been seen as an indication of strength and maturity. The wisdom of knowing that all of us have to find our own places in the Canadian sunlight makes me hopeful that these series of proposals, once engaged, will give us all the opportunity to participate in the building of Canada.
Thomas D'Arcy McGee, who was a son of Ireland but who became a father of Canada, saw a brilliant future for our country. Seven years before Confederation he said: "I look to the future of my adopted country with hope, though not without anxiety. I see in the not remote distance one great nationality, bound like the shield of Achilles by the blue rim of ocean. I see it quartered into many communities, each disposing of its internal affairs, but all bound together by free institutions, free intercourse and free commerce. I see within the round of that shield the peaks of the western mountains and the crests of the eastern waves. I see a generation of industrious, contented men and women free in name and in fact, capable of maintaining in peace and in war a constitution worthy of such a great country."

Mr. Speaker, along with all other members of this House in all political parties, I too see such a country, a country of women and men, of your children and mine whose standard of living is the envy of millions and whose way of life is admired around the world. This country Canada, the second largest country on earth, is also according to the United Nations one of the two best countries in the world in which to live. The challenge for us now is to make Canada second to none.
The challenge is to build a stronger country for the security and the prosperity of all Canadians. I have said in this House on other occasions that the job of nation building did not end with Confederation, and had the Fathers of Confederation sought perfection and insisted on perfection there would have been no Canada in 1867. That was the beginning of nation building, but it continues with each generation and it continues to this day in our minds and in our hearts.
As McGee said, we want a Constitution cherished in the hearts of all of its people, not part of its people, not some of its people, not the people who live in the west and the east but English speaking Canadians, French speaking Canadians, from the north, the south and the east-all Canadians are deserving of a Constitution that represents them and reflects their hopes and dreams and aspirations for a new and a better Canada.
We have the challenge to keep Canada and today we have the opportunity to improve it. Nothing would serve the economic interests of all Canadians more directly than clear resolution of constitutional challenges. They have bedevilled this nation for too long. I think that it would be with a sense of national relief and gratitude that all Canadians dealt with a proposal that managed to bring this to a successful conclusion.
In that spirit I invite all Canadians, all political parties that believe in one undiminished Canada, to set aside other differences and to engage in nation building with the full exuberance that this magnificent country deserves.
I suggest that we get on with it, the building of Canada, of a vision of Macdonald and Cartier and McGee, and the country of our own dreams, a new Canada for a new century, honoured in the family of nations as a modern and flexible and caring country, a Canada respected by its peers, a Canada loved by its people, a Canada better able to serve its citizens with governments and institutions revised and reformed by this Parliament and by all
Routine Proceedings
Canadians that will be tied to the very best that Canada can provide.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in this House today very conscious of the importance of the issue before us. At a time of significant national debate, each of us must fulfil our duties to the best of our abilities.
At a time when there is cynicism about the role of politicians, it is particularly important that the political process works the way it should.
I want it to be very clear that the role of the opposition is not to give a blank cheque to the government, nor is it our role to oppose simply for the sake of opposing something. The role of the opposition is to scrutinize, to ask the right questions, to propose improvements and to seek to correct errors. The role of the opposition is to speak for those who have no voice. This is a role that we will fulfil in the months ahead.
I want to say that our objective is the unity of the country, but this does not mean that we will necessarily agree with all of the proposals of the government. Indeed, our first impression is that the proposals of the government need a great deal of work.
Over the next few months some of the debates will be about issues of principle, and we will fight for our principles by proposing improvements, but much of the debate will also be about legal text.
What does one word mean? What does one phrase mean? Are there flaws that can be corrected or improvements that can be made?

Mr. Speaker, a constitution is both a political statement and a legal document. It embodies and reflects the values Canadians share and defines the legal structure of our society.
Unlike other arrangements such as collective bargaining agreements and trade agreements which are temporary and easy to amend, a constitution is not easy to change, and that is as it should be.
When dealing with fundamental values, with political institutions, with the delicate balance of a society, our approach must be considered and prudent. Since the changes we make will be with us for a long time, it is preferable to get the wording right before the proposals are agreed to.

Routine Proceedings

As a legal document which individuals, governments and the courts must rely upon, it must accurately reflect the intention of its authors.
Let us resolve not to transform a debate on legal meaning of proposals into an emotional debate about rejections and humiliations. Let us not transform a debate about values into a lot of empty rhetoric and political posturing.
Clearly it is too early for anyone to state definitively a hard and fast position on the government paper. Constitutional language is extremely important and some of the government papers lack legal precision. In many places we do not have a specific proposal, just a list of options.
Over the coming weeks and months, with the help of the people of Canada, we in this party will work to find specific answers. In this round we will not tolerate constitutional wording which is so deliberately ambiguous that it can be used to mean one thing in one part of Canada and something else in another part of the country.
Ensuring that these proposals are thoroughly debated, thoroughly reviewed and where necessary amended, abandoned or enlarged-that is our duty. It is a duty we in this party will honour. We will not compromise on principles.

As the Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada, I promise to do my best to ensure that all Canadians can take part in the debate on the proposals for constitutional reform. The Constitution does not belong to the politicians or the bureaucrats. The Constitution belongs to the people.
Hear, hear!

I need not remind the Prime Minister of the failure of Parliament's last attempt at constitutional reform. This attempt failed because the Canadian people were excluded from the debate. It was the wrong approach.
The Charter of Rights and Freedoms, enshrined in the Constitution in 1982 to embody the common heritage of all Canadians, was the result of long and passionate public debate and of negotiations between governments. The most progressive provisions in the Charter, including protection of the rights of the disabled and measures to help disadvantaged groups, were made as a result of public hearings.
Quebecers know how important it is to have a Charter of Rights because they drafted their own charter several years ago. The Quebec Charter has influenced to a considerable extent the Charter that is now part of the Canadian Constitution.
Canadians have a stake in the Constitution, and they feel they are its guardians. The constitutional debate is not the exclusive preserve of politicians and bureaucrats. If it is to be credible and command respect, the debate must involve the people of this country.
On April 21, I urged the government to produce detailed and concrete proposals for constitutional reform that would immediately be considered by a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons. We recommended that the committee hold public hearings to receive the views, advice and comments of individuals, experts, groups and governments.
I said at the time that tabling concrete proposals would make it possible for all provincial governments, including the Government of Quebec, to express their views and to seek agreement with the federal government on the substance of the reform. We recommended that the committee be authorized to make recommendations aimed at amending and improving the proposals to reflect the opinions expressed, and that seems to have been accepted.
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely hope the committee will make every attempt to involve the people in this debate. I also hope that committee members will work together to seek a genuine compromise.

The lessons of Meech Lake are written for all to see. The people shall never be ignored. I will hold the Prime Minister to his promise made today before the entire nation, his promise to involve the people of Canada in this new round.
September 24, 1991

This joint parliamentary committee is to report at the end of February. We must use the remaining time to study the proposals, to debate their meaning, to consult widely and to listen to the people of Canada.
I have spent time talking about the process because the process is very important. Now I will address principles which are equally important.
One of Canada's greatest constitutional thinkers, the late Professor F. R. Scott, once wrote:
If Canadians can agree upon great and lasting principles upon
which they wish their society to be built, then they can agree upon the
broad outlines of a Constitution to achieve these ends.
Our principles as Liberals are clear:
(1)	What is proposed must be compatible with the very nature of Canada, a nation which finds its raison d'etre in sharing diversity and respect for the rights of individuals.
(2)	The solutions proposed must result in real reform of our political institutions to ensure that the distinct concern of Canada's regions are respected.
(3)	The solution proposed must recognize the need to renew and modernize our economic instruments, including the training and mobility of our work force to create policies that will permit us to be competitive in the world of tomorrow.
(4)	Constitutional reform must not weaken the right of individuals as guaranteed in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
(5)	Constitutional reform must not weaken the Canadian duality, nor the rights of official language minorities everywhere in Canada.
(6)	Constitutional reform must not weaken Canada's cultural diversity and its heritage of tolerance.
(7)	Constitutional reform must not weaken the ability of a strong federal government to speak and act for all Canadians.
The Liberal Party of Canada entered this debate convinced that the things we call Canadian values are as relevant today as they have been at any time in our history. At a time when Canadian values are under attack and when our country is divided as never before, we believe that Canadians must remind themselves of the greatness of the Canadian experiment. We also believe that Canadians must devote their energies to finding new bonds and new endeavours which reflect our
Routine Proceedings
collective values. We must concentrate now on what unites us, and not what divides us.
More than ever we must commit ourselves to true Canadian values, values like generosity of spirit and collective action, values that will permit us to meet the next century with our head held high.
In discussing constitutional reform, we must reflect on the great and lasting principles of our society. Constitutional reforms must have one goal and only one goal, that is the well-being not of governments, not of politicians, not of bureaucrats, but of the citizens of Canada.
Which government holds which power only matters inasmuch as citizens are well served. Therefore, to serve the citizens of Canada, and that is what all of us have been elected to do, we must understand the values we share as Canadians. After all, Canadian citizenship means more than a shared passport. It is shared values. Quite frankly, Canadian citizens have a right to a government that can speak and act for all Canadians.
As Canadians we have a unique and profound commitment to a shared sense of social responsibility. We believe in equality and equality of opportunity. We respect the individual and we also have a very strong sense of obligation to the community as a whole. We believe that we are responsible for each other. We believe it is our responsibility, every one of us, to ensure that Canadians, wherever they live, enjoy a Canadian quality of life.
The partnership of French-speaking and Englishspeaking Canadians built a nation where French is not spoken only in Quebec. I am very proud to be in this House today and to have been elected in a riding where the majority of the people are Acadian and I am very proud that they speak French-

[-] that they speak French, that they are truly French even if they do not live in Quebec and want to remain French-speaking within all of Canada.

I am proud to be in a country where English is not restricted to the other nine provinces. There are a lot of people in my province of Quebec who are as much Quebecers as anyone of us and who are English speaking

Routine Proceedings
and deserve to be protected like anybody else. That is a fundamental cornerstone of what we call Canada.
I want to state clearly that we will not accept any constitutional change that will effectively split Canada into two nations, nine English provinces on one side, and a French Quebec on the other side.
Canada's aboriginal peoples are a fundamental characteristic of our country too. But at the same time the treatment of aboriginal citizens is also a test. It is a test of our values. It is a test that we have failed in the past. We must not fail again in the years ahead. We have built a country that has welcomed people from every comer of the world. Diversity and multiculturalism, the fact that we can be different and be Canadian too, are fundamental characteristics of Canada.

These values form the foundation upon which to build our constitutional reform proposals. The Canadian Constitution recognizes the importance of the individual. Thus it protects the fundamental rights and freedoms of every citizen.
It recognizes our two official languages and acknowledges formally multiculturalism. It protects the rights of the aboriginal people of Canada. It recognizes the principle of equalization which ensures that all regions of Canada are afforded equal opportunities.
The Constitution grants provincial governments great autonomy and considerable power. In itself, the Canadian federal system has promoted the development of provinces all distinct from one another. Quebec as we know it today and are all so proud of developed within this Canadian federation.
We also recognized that Canada is far more than the sum of its parts, far more that just a community of communities. A strong national government has always been necessary to meet the great challenges we face today. More than ever a strong national government is needed if we are to meet the global challenges of tomorrow, especially in the 21st century.
So, Mr. Speaker, this is a strong foundation upon which we can build. We do not have to start from scratch. We must improve upon what we have.

Let me repeat, Mr. Speaker. We have in this party recognized that Canada is far more than the sum of its parts. It is far more than a community of communities. A strong national government has always been necessary to meet the great challenges we face today. A strong national government will remain necessary to meet the global challenges we will encounter in the months and years ahead.
The Liberal Party will not compromise on this principle. Our approach to constitutional change will be guided by this principle. Let me be clear, Mr. Speaker. In Canada we have a strong foundation upon which to build the future. We do not have to rebuild our nation from scratch. Instead, we must improve upon what we already have.

Over the last several months, we in the Liberal Party of Canada have made public the kind of country we hope to build in the months and years to come. We are, I am proud to say, the first federal political party to have made their intentions known to the Canadian people.
I have made it clear that Canada must not stand still in an ever changing world. To maintain the status quo is not good enough. Most countries are making changes in their institutions to adapt to the requirements of the next century. I suggest that Canada must not be the exception.

I set out the objectives of the Liberal Party on constitutional reform in Montreal on April 21. They will guide us in our work over the next few months. Let me repeat them here in the House of Commons.
First, we propose that the Constitution include an inspiring declaration of the nature of Canada. This declaration would set out the will of Canadians to live together in a federal state, the principles which govern that state, the values we share, our commitment to two official languages, a recognition of our diverse cultural heritage, a recognition of the distinctiveness of Quebec and a recognition of the role of the aboriginal peoples.

The government has tabled such a declaration. We will examine its wording and propose improvements where necessary.
Second, a commitment to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. All Canadians have a strong attachment to the fundamental rights and freedoms found in the Charter. They want to see those freedoms strengthened. In the Liberal Party, our position is very clear. We will not accept any constitutional change that diminishes the rights and freedoms of Canadians protected by the Charter. We will not accept that.
Third, strengthening the Canadian economic union. In the Canadian federal state we are entitled to expect the full benefits associated with the unrestricted mobility of people, goods, services and capital. This is essential if we are to develop internationally competitive products, services and technologies, things we need to meet the demands of globalization.
Then we 'need to break down interprovincial trade barriers. Those barriers are coming down all over the world and we must break them down in Canada as well. The government has made some proposals in this area. Our first reaction is that they need to be strengthened. There appears to be too many loopholes. We will be recommending a number of major improvements.
Fourth, institutional reform. The regions of Canada need to be more involved in decision making and policy making at the national level. To meet the hopes and dreams of those who live in the west and the Atlantic, a reformed Senate is essential. It must be a Senate that is elected, effective and equitable. Such a Senate should have the power to examine appointments to important federal institutions and agencies. It should also protect the rights of minority language groups, and it should require a double majority for legislation touching upon the French language and culture.
It appears that the government has adopted a lot of this proposal. We will listen carefully to the view expressed before the committee.

Fifth, concerning the division of powers, constitutional reform involves the redistribution of powers. That is inescapable.
The criterion should be the following: jurisdiction must be granted to the level of government in the best position to exercise it. A functional approach should be used.
We must seek the arrangement that will best serve the interests of the people rather than that of governments, bureaucrats or politicians. The new arrangements must be flexible enough to meet the challenges that lay ahead.
There are a number of areas in which the federal and provincial governments should be able to pass complementary legislation. For instance, we should be able to adopt national environmental standards and let the provinces adapt these standards to regional requirements.
The government's approach to the question of power sharing seems to be to give up federal powers to the provinces, without getting anything in exchange.
We intend to scrutinize each proposal in the light of our principles, in other words, it must be functional, and there must be a national government able to act and speak for all Canadians. We will draft amendments as appropriate and submit them to the committee.
I would also like to discuss the subject of spending powers. We believe it should be possible to limit the federal government's spending power in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. In the past, the problem was how to reconcile restrictions on spending power and the need for national standards. A functional redistribution of powers would help limit spending power without compromising national standards. However, it is essential that by the end of February, we do not end up with two Canadas, one rich, with first class social services, and one poor, with second class social services.
There is also an administrative agreement between Ottawa and Quebec that governs immigration. This agreement must be made part of the Constitution. The government appears to have accepted the proposals we made in Montreal last April.

I want to raise some questions particularly on the proposed economic union. I believe we can all agree in this House that the reduction of trade barriers, that greater co-operation among provinces and territories, is an important and laudable goal, but we must ask some hard questions.
Does the kind of domestic free trade in people, goods, finance and capital extend the same laissez-faire principles of the Canada-U.S. trade deal to a domestic playing field? Will there be winners and losers in this and, if so, how do we deal with that? Could this potentially lead to a whole new round of privatization, deregulation, diminishing social standards and diminishing corporate taxes as we look at this in terms of greater co-operation?
We must raise questions about the ability within Canada to reach the goals that we wish to reach in this economic co-operation if we in fact do not have a transportation infrastructure in place, which is absolutely necessary in a country of this size and which lamentably has been systematically destroyed.
What does the right of corporations to free movement of goods, services and capital mean for weaker provinces that seek to establish their own economic development programs? What does it mean for provincial Crown
corporations? What does it mean for provinces or territories trying to support local jobs and fledgling industries? What does it mean for affirmative action? What are the implications of this form of economic union in terms of aboriginal self-government agreements?
Economic union that only addresses control and harmonization but does not mention initiatives to have greater regional equality and to strengthening section 36 of the Constitution on regional equality falls far short in this party's opinion.
Economic union proposals which suggest that the only role of the Bank of Canada will be to address inflation, not as well to look at unemployment, to look at fiscal and monetary policies as an instrument to address unemployment, fall far short of what we can be and can do if we are to have greater co-operation in the economy across this country.
While we support greater co-operation and while we support looking at a renewal of the relationships among the provinces, territories and the federal government in economic areas, we must also not simply take a defensive posture but a posture that says in this economy that we will reach out, that we will initiate to seek greater equality, and that that will be a strong commitment of a federal government, any federal government of any political party, and a fundamental part of our Constitution.

The hon. member for Dartmouth has three minutes left.

Mr. Speaker, I usually cannot say my name in three minutes, but I will do my best to try to conclude by contribution to this debate on this very regressive piece of legislation, Bill C-32.
Yesterday I focused my opposition to this particular piece of legislation by using some examples of what this government's economic policies have done to some of the poorest parts of this country, particularly Atlantic Canada. At that time one of the members opposite indicated, at least I heard them mutter from across the aisle: "This is not going to affect Nova Scotia. You are not one of the have provinces, where there is going to be a cap put on CAP".
Just because you come from a have not province does not mean that you do not have enough good and caring left in your heart and concern for this country that you cannot get up in this Chamber and speak for those you, perhaps, do not represent legitimately as a member of Parliament from a particular riding, but you do represent as a member of the Liberal party in this Chamber. There are a lot of Nova Scotians and Newfoundlanders in Ontario and Alberta and other parts of this country who are going to be affected very badly by this piece of legislation.
In Bill C-32, the government is attempting to put a cap on CAP, the assistance that is given to the poorest of the poor, the dispossessed, those who are down on their luck. It would do us all very well to just reflect for a minute on what this is going to mean.
There is nowhere in this country, rich or poor province, where the level of municipal social assistance that is paid does anything but keep the recipient of that social assistance and their family absolutely entrenched in a cycle of poverty. In this country an individual who finds himself in need of support and has to rely on a provincial or a municipal government for assistance has nowhere else to go to get enough to feed his family, have
adequate housing, to be able to clothe his children and to be able to feel that he is contributing.
What this bill effectively does is rob those provinces that are affected by this piece of legislation of the ability to enhance social assistance payments. Every member here, probably every weekend when they get home and hold office hours, has somebody in-and I know I only have a minute-but I want to use an example that was used yesterday by my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier. It is a startling statistic.
According to Statistics Canada, if you have a family of four with two parents working at minimum wage-working at minimum wage-those individuals live below the poverty line in this country. We are talking about the working poor. Another startling statistic is that in 1988 there are nearly one million children who are living in poverty.
In conclusion I want to say that this bill will do absolutely nothing but ensure that those who find themselves in that despair will find that their despair and misery will increase.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague from Dartmouth who showed not only the goodness in his heart in speaking on behalf of his colleagues from the three provinces involved, but also to draw to the attention of the House, and indeed to the viewing audience, that we in the Atlantic region are not so concerned with our own province that we can't look at the country at large. But I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that as I stand on my feet today, I would think that the hon. member for Dartmouth, despite the largesse of his heart is probably more concerned about Atlantic Canada right now. And it is that sort of thing that has caused us to rise to this occasion.
I would like to ask the hon. member for his comment on the following aspect of this, which quite frankly has bothered me for some time and continues to bother me. Presumably, this bill is the government's response to try and reduce the debt, by transferring the debt of the national government to the provinces. I can understand that as a cost saving measure, but quite frankly I am getting a little sick and tired of hearing the government from across the floor blame this debt on Liberal policies.
I think after seven years of trying to run the country it
September 24, 1991

should now have another system of trying to find the reasons for why we are in this condition that we are in right now.
I know the member campaigned-we met a couple of times during the campaign for the 1988 election. Mr. Speaker, I recall quite well promises being made, and in particular the promise of child care, for I think it was around $4 billion. This government, as one of its election promises, was very adamant that it had a program and it was prepared to look at it, and it even put a cost figure on it of $4 billion. I mention that, not as a specific program, although I was very concerned about that.
But I was also concerned that there was another $8 billion of promises. I was somewhat concerned about this, because while the public debt was not a major issue at the time, certainly not when the government was campaigning, I think most Canadians were concerned with that. I recall the Minister of Finance of the day saying that: "These are not campaign promises; they are in the program. We are going to spend that money. They are commitments".
Mr. Speaker, days after-in fact, I think it was in the next budget after the election and this government's first budget-there was no sign of child care. There was no sign of child care in the next budget or many other of these promises, not the least of which was a prison in my riding that was clearly an election promise, though I expect it will start to surface again as one of their promises.
I would like to ask the hon. member for Dartmouth for his comment and his feeling on these kinds of promises that are made, on the one hand, and on the other hand trying to cut back and blaming it on the Liberals because "we now have to transfer all these debts that we can't manage to the provinces".

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague has raised some very salient points. As members from provinces that are have not provinces at this time, to try to keep us from yelling too loudly against this bill, the government has said; "Don't worry about it, because it is not going to affect you, and you, of course, can trust us when we tell you that".
This is what it goes back to, a matter of trust. I remember clearly during the 1988 campaign that this government opposite also made a number of other
Government Orders
promises dealing with the well-being of families and the fiscal ability of families to make a living. One of them was child care. We remember that anybody who campaigned in that election said that child care was not a promise; it was a commitment. We also heard that regional development was not a promise; it was a commitment. We also heard that real tax reform that would save people money was not a promise; it was a commitment.
Just as with the prison in the hon. member's riding, we all found out very soon after the election that those commitments were written with disappearing ink. It is little wonder that people on our side of the House who stand with the majority of Canadians in opposing this piece of legislation say: "No, no, don't tell us now this is a measure that is only going to take place until these guys opposite can get their fiscal house in order. We do not believe them for a minute. Do not tell us that Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, the Northwest Territories, Saskatchewan, Manitoba or Quebec is not going to be nailed by the broadening and deepening of this particular regressive piece of legislation, because we simply do not believe them".
The record of this Conservative government in fooling or misleading the people intentionally or unintentionally during campaigns is there for all to see. The Progressive Conservative government gets up in this House and indicates that this is necessary for fiscal responsibility.
"The economy is in really good shape", do you remember, Mr. Speaker, during the campaign? I certainly do in Atlantic Canada. My hon. colleague from Newfoundland remembers. The Prime Minister went around and promised that he was going to cause prosperity to break out all over, to inflict prosperity on this country.
He certainly has not inflicted it on the Atlantic fisheries. My hon. colleague from Newfoundland probably spends most of his working day. It is a long day when he goes back to his constituency, having to deal with the economic chaos caused by this government's policy in dealing with the Atlantic fisheries.
When I go home to my riding I have to deal with individuals who are living below the poverty line. Every time they make a purchase they are paying the GST on it.
