In conclusion, I want to reaffirm and agree with my hon. colleague that this is the thin edge of the wedge. This government is absolutely not credible when it comes to making promises on fiscal responsibility and prosperity.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to tell my colleague that I am a little confused by the explanations given to us by the government. Perhaps he could clarify this for us.
We heard during the last election campaign that campaign promises were different than commitments, but the net effect has been that both the commitments and the promises were broken.
I ask my colleague whether he recognizes the difference between a Tory promise and a Tory commitment, because I cannot.
Mr. Speaker, quite simply there is no difference. They are both worthless.
Hear, hear.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, I feel honoured to rise to speak after the hon. member for Dartmouth who has made such a fine and cogent presentation. In fact, I would rather not follow him because it is always very difficult to follow his dynamic and outstanding presentations in this House. I am sure his constituents are very proud of him this morning.
I want to address this again because while the hon. member did speak well it was the last part of the presentation that was started yesterday. To assist in the flow and continuity, and quite frankly to refresh myself on this, I would like to make it clear what the purpose of this bill is.
Oh, oh.

The hon. member from across the floor laughs.
There have been so many bills dealing with a number of items that I would like to find out if Bill C-32 is in fact a bill to cap what is called the Canada Assistance Plan and applies to the three richest provinces in the country: Alberta, British Columbia, and Ontario.
Some people may ask, and those in my riding who are watching me may ask: "Why is the member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception speaking on problems in Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario?"
There are two answers to that. One is that as a member of Parliament I am very conscious that I am a member in this House and represent primarily my riding. Certainly the last couple of months has been very focused on the disastrous fishing we have had and the effort on the part of me and my colleagues, and indeed the whole Liberal Party and caucus, in trying to get the government to address that problem now, not two or three months later or weeks later. People are without money and they are hurting now.
While that is a major concern, as a federal member I feel it incumbent, in representing my riding and my constituents, to speak on behalf of Canada and to be involved in things like the constitutional debate that we heard this morning and to concern myself about measures that are taken by this government, whether they apply to Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, Newfoundland or to the rest of Canada.
The second reason is the primary reason. The primary reason is that cutting off or reducing the assistance programs to these people and these provinces in which, by the way, quite a large percentage of Newfoundlanders live, indeed from my riding, will indeed affect them as I will later point out. It is very important to understand that these provinces that get what is called the Canadian Assistance Program for which this bill is meant do not receive federal equalization payments like we do in Newfoundland.
I want to express my concern for the equalization payments that were cut off to the Atlantic provinces because they are equal to this cap that is now being put on the Canadian Assistance Program. By way of illustration, I want to relate to you, to this House and to my colleagues, just what the transfer of payments and the restriction have done in my province and in my riding.
I do not want to go through the revelation again of pointing out the promises that were made. Indeed, one promise shortly after this government was elected was to reduce the deficit despite 22 income tax increases in that time and the imposition of the despicable and hated goods and services tax at a time it could not have been worse, not only for the economy of Newfoundland and Atlantic Canada but for the rest of the country. This was at a time when there was a made-in-Canada recession
September 24, 1991

that this government admitted to finally after being cajoled and reasoned by other members on this side of the House.
On top of all that, then, was a measure-and to me it was a despicable measure and a measure that I was not comfortable with-to to reduce the debt on a national basis. Basically this government is giving up the responsibility that traditionally the federal Government of Canada as a strong central government has had for those difficulties in the economy and those regions in Canada that were hurt the most.
That was one of the reasons this country was formed in 1867. It was, from a central viewpoint, to be able to cope with the problems that regions had. As each province joined then there was a better ability on the part of the central government to handle these regional problems. I very much regret that the government is divesting itself of that responsibility. It bothers me tremendously.
Since I have been a member of Parliament I recall the 1989 budget. Although it did not particularly contain great CAP measures or reductions in transfer payments, at that particular point in time it did close various parts of Atlantic Canada. I think VIA Rail was concerned and other measures mitigated tremendously against the economy. Then in 1990 there was a signal from the budget that we would have difficulties in transfer payments and in particular the 1991 February budget extended the freeze on the transfer payments to the budget year 1994-95. There had been a two-year freeze from the previous budget, and then in February we saw a freeze for another three years.
This came on the heels of lower payments in other areas. It came at a time when we were trying to standardize levels of service. It came at a time when the economy of the country was heading downhill and the economy of Atlantic Canada, because of the reduction in the economy due to poor fishing in Newfoundland and other factors in the rest of the province, became a major concern. On the heels of this dismal economic outlook, we had inflicted on us the reduction in transfer payments.
Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, I think you would appreciate, as all members of the House would, that it is very difficult to get a precise dollar figure on this because it is based on certain projections that would determine what the transfer payments would have been if this restriction had not been placed.
A figure that certainly I see recurring-I can agree more or less with this figure-is that the activation of the reduction of transfer payments as it applies to the provinces other than the three being considered by this bill is in Newfoundland, $148.6 million in the last three fiscal years; Prince Edward Island, $33.8 million; Nova Scotia, $230.8 million; and New Brunswick, $167.3 million.
It may be higher now because of economic factors, but as far as I and my colleagues are concerned the net effect of these developments has been to erode Ottawa's contribution to provincial treasuries in the Atlantic region rather severely.
To give some indication of the totality of what this means, we in Newfoundland, and indeed those in the rest of Atlantic Canada, rely largely on the central government and on these Ottawa transfer payments for a percentage of our annual budget.
The net result of what was done, the subject that is being discussed right now, is that the proportion of [DOT]Newfoundland's total current account, the revenues in the budget of last year coming from federal resources, was down from 50 per cent in the previous year to about 45 per cent.
That is a 5 per cent reduction. That is incredible. Corresponding figures applied for Prince Edward Island, for Nova Scotia and for New Brunswick.
I do not have to point out to anybody who is listening to this from the Atlantic region the downstream effect that this has had. Irrespective of the stripe, colour and kind of government, they have had tremendous difficulties in coping with the financial difficulty that this has transferred to their government, to their caucuses and cabinets and eventually to their people.
The net effect of this cap has been the same, because these transfer payments are essentially meant to assist those who need it the most.

September 24, 1991
Government Orders
The CAP program per se, as I see it, helps those who are helped in a similar manner by the transfer payments. I am looking at health, social assistance and, to a certain extent, education.

Mr. Speaker, among those who benefit from the Canada Assistance Plan and the other social services are, firstly, the children who need protection because they suffer from abuse or neglect, but also the handicapped, whether physically or mentally, single parent families, older persons, the unemployed, families and individuals in distress, low-income workers and battered women.

CAP is the main component of Canada's social safety net. We have heard that so many times that I think it means so much to so many people. It is the last resource for those who have exhausted or have been denied all other forms of financial assistance.
In 1988 and 1989 for which there are solid figures this program benefited 1.853 million Canadians from the social assistance provisions. Now 46 per cent of these recipients live in British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario which are the provinces that would be affected by CAP. This was related and spoken to in great lengths when Bill C-69 was being discussed. The inadequacy of social assistance benefits is a leading cause of child poverty in Canada.
I do want to return to something that I spoke about earlier here this morning. I did indulge the House to a certain extent and was supported by my hon. colleague from Dartmouth in his presentation of his concern. I have to reflect on the difficulty I have with a government that is trying to convey the impression that it is caring, that it is concerned, and that the needs and the cares of the ordinary person matter to them.
I would attribute and I would ascribe that concern to them because I know a lot of the members across the floor of the House. I deal with them on a regular and hopefully often a non-partisan basis, people like yourself, Mr. Speaker. I know that as individuals there are caring people on the other side of the House. But I have some difficulty understanding how that is translated from the individual concerns to the government as a group of people trying to run the country. I do not know how much influence the caring members have but there are many examples of that.
Mr. Speaker, I will give you one example. While it may not be directly related to caps, transfer payments and equalization payments, it certainly is a concern that we see every day. I have seen it every day. In particular, I have seen it since about May of this year.
I am not unlike any other member. I am not going to stand up here and take credit for travelling through my riding extensively. Every member pretty well does that, any members that are worth their salt. It is one thing to hear about it on the radio. It is something else to go and talk to an individual and say: "What kind of a year are you having?" We do this not only to listen to their words but to see the look on their faces, to see the despair, the emotion, and to talk to their families-their wives, fathers, mothers, brothers and sisters-to see the difficulty they have in coming to grips with just the thought that no one really cares to the point where they are prepared to do something for them.
I wish it were otherwise that I had to stand up here and ask for assistance from the government for the people whom I am responsible for in Bonavista-Trinity-Conception. In the first instance we had a situation in Newfoundland where the ice conditions were extraordinary. I have a background in marine subjects. I have spent essentially a lifetime at sea. I am from a family that has spent a long time at sea. I am from a province that has a seagoing heritage which needs no amplification here.
I have never seen a year like this. In the memory of those people to whom I speak, they have never seen a year like it either. Fishing normally starts in May, cod fishing. This year, May came, no fishing; June came, no fishing. In fact every week fishermen were trying to get their nets out and catch some fish, essentially cod, and they could not even get their nets out. When they got their nets out they were destroyed.
I will have to say that the government eventually did come up with a rescue package the day before this House closed on June 18,1 believe it was. It was for $18 million.
I am grateful for that and my people are grateful for that.
However, every single day and every single week there were questions in the House of Commons. The people who finally got some assistance had to go through a living hell to get that. They did not know they were going to get it. Every day I would get 40 to 50 telephone calls toward the end saying: "When is something going to be done for us?" Eventually there was recognition that something
September 24, 1991

had to be done and eventually there was consideration shown.
The point I want to make is that the human anxiety people went through before this aid package was given was something that I am physically and mentally incapable of portraying to this House of Commons. Equally, beyond that we are in the same position, except it is worse because more people are involved and the financial constraints and financial implications are even worse. I am going down to my riding this weekend and I know I am going to be speaking to yet more fishermen, more plant workers and plant owners. Everybody in the riding is affected by that. They are asking me: "When is something going to happen?"
Most of them have seen me and my other colleagues in the House ask the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister of Employment and Immigration when something was going to be done for these people. Their answer is: "We are working on something and we will let you know when it is ready".
I cannot go back to my riding and tell people: "Well, I cannot do any more because the government is not ready yet". My responsibility, as I see it, is to explain the problems of my riding to this government and not to go back and explain to Bonavista-Trinity-Conception why this government has a particular policy.
In other words, I am here to express the policies and concerns of my constituents to this government and not to go explain government policy back to my constituents. I have to do it sometimes, particularly when it affects them. Surely, it has to be a two-way street and surely my responsibility is primarily to represent them in explaining to this government what their problems are instead of going back and saying to them: "This government has a problem because it has not been able to reduce the national debt despite 22 tax increases, the goods and services tax, the cutbacks on VIA Rail and the cutbacks on this and that".
The cutback in Atlantic Canada, in my province, is such that one has to live in the United States to call a toll-free number to cross on the ferry. If one lives in Newfoundland one cannot call a toll-free number to
Government Orders
make a reservation to go across the gulf either from Argentia or from Port aux Basques. That is totally unacceptable. It is totally uncaring. It is a small thing, but it irks people. They believe that somebody up here, the governing party, really does not care about them.
I see that my time is coming to a close. I want in closing to make three final points.
The first point is that for all the reasons I and and my other colleagues have mentioned, we in the Liberal caucus are consistently opposed to this limit on the Canada Assistance Program.
Second, we do not support the measure that transfers the burden of national debt and the federal deficit reduction on to the backs of poor Canadians. Why should rich Canadians pay for poor Canadians? That is not the concept of this country. That is not what we believe in. That is certainly not what I believe in, as an individual who represents people who are not rich.
Finally, while the government may have the legal right because of a Supreme Court judgment to cut welfare payments to the provinces, I do not believe there is a moral right to abandon its responsibilities to poor and disadvantaged Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of Parliament from Kootenay East, British Columbia, I feel compelled to speak out against this regressive legislation. It is no wonder that we do not see in the House Conservative members from British Columbia getting up and supporting this piece of legislation. That is because it is a cutback in social programs for the province of British Columbia. As a member of Parliament who represents an interior area where many people are subjected to having to use and apply for social assistance, I find this very offensive.
Just for a moment I want to refer back to the last election. As we went through the campaign the free trade debate was the big debate that was going on across Canada. We heard our Prime Minister tell the people of Canada, who were concerned about our social programs, our safety nets on our health and welfare programs and our medicare, that it was a sacred trust and we did not have to worry about it.

Government Orders
I want to say that they do have something to worry about. We have seen the changes to our Unemployment Insurance Act. We have seen the changes to our hospitals and so on. We have seen the waiting lists of people trying to get into hospitals and so on. We have seen the cuts in post-secondary education. Now we see Bill C-32, an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in British Columbia, in Alberta and in Ontario. The rationale of this government is that these are richer provinces, that they can afford it and that it is going to bring about some fiscal changes to the government and try to assist it in its debt.
I want to say to the House and to Canadians that the people who require social assistance do not look at British Columbia as being any richer than any other province. The need is there, the requirement is there, as some of the people in the government would know if they were to sit in some of these offices and hear the problems as I do in my riding with social assistance and the food banks. I visit the food banks. What does this message tell the food banks out there tiying to bring a bit of added assistance to people so that they can live a little better? Many of them are single women, many of them are children of single parent families, and so on. What does this message tell the food banks out there volunteering their efforts to try to make their lives a little better?
I want to say that the government is not admiring the work they are doing. It is saying to them: "We are going to make it even harder for you and you are going to have to go out there and beg further and further to try to assist these people".
While this has been going on, the government has brought in changes to our taxation system. It brought in a consumers' tax, a 7 per cent added tax so that even the people who are prepared to share a little more through the food bank systems are finding it harder and harder for themselves. The Unemployment Insurance Act has been changed and people are finding it harder and harder to qualify and to live on unemployment insurance payments. The post-secondary education clauses are being changed and our students who want to go to school and want to carry on are finding that they cannot.
This summer while I was sitting in my office and we were running into the fall session where students were beginning to want to qualify for student loans-and I am talking about a loan; I am not talking about a grant-they would come in to my office and say that they had difficulty getting through.
As a member of Parliament I thought that should not be any problem. I picked up the phone and I phoned the office in Vancouver time after time and that line was busy the whole time. When a member of Parliament cannot get through on the phone to talk to the department, it shows that this government is cutting back even in the areas of answering the telephone to try to assist people. I am finding the same thing throughout the various programs.
I look back at some of the problems I see with social assistance in my riding, where young children of 17 or 18 years of age have difficulty at home and find themselves in situations where they feel they are being abused. They are coming in to my office and I am going down to social assistance trying to find places for these people, and it is not being done.
I want to say to the government, and especially to members of Parliament of this government from British Columbia, that they have a responsibility to this province. They should not allow the government to cut back universality in our social programs, in our medicare programs, in our unemployment insurance programs and in our pension programs. That is what they are doing. The universality of our programs is being attacked in a very mean and cold-hearted way.
I have seen it not only in the social programs. They all affect one another. If we do not have proper health care, if we do not have jobs, if we do not have unemployment insurance, it all reflects back and finally we reach the stage where we come under the social assistance programs.
As the former mayor of a municipality, I want to say to the municipalities in British Columbia that they are also under attack. As this affects the province, it comes down into the municipalities and into the regional districts because in cutting back in these areas where the need is the most urgent they are going to find that it will reflect on the way of life of those whole communities.

It is much harder to receive these services because we are at the very extreme end of the province. Many times you have to fly to Vancouver or Calgary in emergencies.
These are some of the problems that we have and it all relates, because it all comes back to our social assistance programs, our medicare program. I had a case in my riding where someone had a very serious attack and needed to fly by helicopter to Calgary. They got halfway to Calgary and were told to return to Cranbrook because they did not qualify under the air ambulance system of that province. They had to fly under the air ambulance service, and they returned that person back to Cranbrook.
Is that the kind of rationale that we are getting into with regard to our services throughout the country? No. We in the New Democratic Party believe in universality. We believe that the poor and the people who require that assistance should be treated equally in every province throughout Canada.
That is not happening. That is not what this legislation says. Bill C-32 allows for the extension of the 5 per cent limit of the Canada Assistance Plan for the provinces of B.C., Alberta and Ontario. That is not universality. I say to this government; get back to the people. Is it any wonder that your government is running so low in the polls?
I see members from British Columbia sitting there, not getting up and standing up for the rights of our British Columbia people. I want to say to them; stand up and try to defend this piece of legislation because we have an election going on in British Columbia at the present time and the people of British Columbia will want to know where this government stands with regard to the social assistance programs in our province.
This government has a responsibility as a federal government. If the government is not capable of supplying jobs for the people and is not capable of allowing them to go to school to further their education, then surely to goodness we must have programs in place so that they can at least send their children to school with some dignity.
I do not want to leave the thought that there is any dignity in the meagre amounts of money that is available through social assistance programs because it is a very difficult time for children, single parents and the people who require this assistance to tiy to survive.

Go to the food banks in your riding and stay there on a Wednesday afternoon as I have done. See the people coming in and what their needs are, especially around Christmastime. You see exactly what is going on in your ridings.
I want to say to those British Columbia members that I have no doubt that it is going on in your ridings also.
I experienced a problem in my riding where the mines shut down. There were 800 people unemployed. Right away you might say: "They have unemployment insurance and they have other things," but the effects of that taking place and the impact it has on a community is devastating. It is absolutely devastating.
Without knowing that these kinds of programs are in place, makes it that much worse. For this government to bring about a program that is going to cut this back is just wrong. It is wrong, and the government should be looking in the other direction, to try to ensure that there is work for people, that they are able to live in dignity and earn their wages.
At least have the decency to maintain a social program so that they can continue sending their children to school, clothing their children and feeding them. Do not allow the food banks to have to pick up the extra stress because this government has decided it is going to make the poor and the lower income people suffer.
Also, in the same vein, we have the new changes that the government brought in concerning the UIC. Some of these people came into my office and decided to go on unemployment and upgrade their education so that they would not have to be faced with this problem again. They were told, however, that they did not qualify to go on UIC and upgrade their education.
What are we doing? We are changing legislation that the government wants to get out of so it brings in its unemployment insurance bill which places all of the burden on the workers and on the companies and the government stands idly by and watches things take place. It is all part of the free trade agreement. The people out there know that. The people know that the government is systematically getting out of these programs because of the free trade agreement. This is the first step. It is like the travelling salesman who knocks on the door and the first thing he does is shove his foot in the door. He knows if he can get the first foot in the door that is the first part of his sale. That is what the government is doing here. It is getting its foot in the door, bringing about changes in

Government Orders
these provinces. If it gets away with it, it will then bring about more drastic changes than that.
It does not surprise me that this is the route the government is taking. Everyone knew when the free trade debate was taking place that this was going to be the agenda of the government, to get out of many of these programs and to systematically move out. We have seen it.
Bill C-21 makes UIC harder to get, which makes it run out more quickly and, of course, brings people right back on to the social rolls. Family allowances have been cut back. It again comes back on to the people.
The clawbacks in pensions, less money distributed throughout the communities, cutbacks in the agreements between the provinces; everywhere we look this government has attacked. Where is the child care program that was promised during the election so that single parents, who wanted to get out and obtain another job and increase their method of maintaining their families? It is not available to them.
As I go through the riding, I see that social programs are not meeting the needs of the people at the present time. For this government to bring about a 5 per cent cut in British Columbia is just not acceptable. Yet we see our Conservative members of Parliament from British Columbia sit idly by and allow this to take place.
Mr. Speaker, I know you have a feeling, as I do, for the people in my province and I know that we all must try to bring about fiscal restraint and so on, but there are other ways of bringing about fiscal restraint. The entertainment tax that large businesses and large corporations are allowed to write off is one method of trying to bring about some restraint, but no, this government does not see fit to look at those kinds of proposals. Those people would be their rich friends that they are attacking.
When I read the Ottawa paper on Sunday and I saw an article concerning large buildings that are sitting empty here in Ottawa. But this government has the gall to put forward a program that would say to our people on social
assistance: "We are going to have to cut you back because of fiscal restraint." Here is a building that is not being utilized by this government and the taxpayers of this country are having to pay for it. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that is not good enough. As a member of Parliament from British Columbia, I say that I am deeply saddened that this government would use this kind of approach on the people who can least afford it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by saying something which I think we should all remind ourselves of in this House from time to time, and it is that very few of us are poor. Because we tend not to be poor, we have very little communication and often very little understanding of what it means to be poor.
That gives us an extra obligation every time we debate a bill like this or an issue that affects those with whom we do not have personal connections, to make sure that we endeavour to understand fully and completely the problems that our actions in this House create for others and the effects they create.
I want to say that this bill goes to the very heart of Liberal principles about what Canada is all about and what any civilized society is all about. We believe very much in the value, dignity and worth of every human being and their right to have a society in which each person can develop to the best of their potential and contribute to their society.
We also believe that Canada is a nation based on a philosophy of sharing the tremendous riches we enjoy, riches that are not enjoyed by many nations of the world. We believe in a sharing of those to the benefit of all Canadians so that we can fully prosper in this country and can fully contribute to the prosperity of others.
Those are principles that are very much being violated by this bill that is before the House today. What it says is that if you are strong, well educated, wealthy and able to stand on your own two feet, this society is going to
September 24, 1991

support you. But if you happen to be sick, elderly, poor, unemployed, psychiatrically disabled, or unable for one reason or another to fully care for yourself and to fully compete in a society that cares only about the strongest surviving, then this society has no place for you. That is what this bill is all about.
This country is an economic union, but it is more than that. It is a union of people who share a vision about social justice, about equality, about opportunities, about progressing and about making things better for people, not worse. Here we are taking a step backwards again.
What is being done in this bill is removing money from programs that allow people to participate in society despite short-term, temporary difficulties that make it hard for them to compete in the way others can. But it joins a parcel of actions by the government which show that only the strong and prosperous matter in this government's Canada. It joins actions against health funding in health programs, it joins cuts to education, all of which are essential investments in this generation and in the next generation and in our country. The fewer people we have who are capable of fully participating and fully developing their talents, the poorer our society is, not just those individuals, but all of Canada and all Canadians.
The Canada Assistance Plan represents the government's contribution to the prevention or alleviation of poverty. It also is much more than that. It is very much a contribution to the development of human beings in our society and therefore to the development of Canadian society. What this bill does is penalize those provinces that have been responsible in how they administer their budgets and how they manage. It penalizes those who contribute most to the prosperity of the rest of Canada through the equalization payments. But it penalizes the poorest within those communities. I can tell you, because my riding is perhaps a good example of this.
Being poor and being surrounded by people who live comfortably and well is very difficult and perhaps more difficult because the support services are not there. The support of the entire community is not there for you. People do not like being poor. They do not like being dependent.
I have worked with people in my community and I have found that it takes so little to break the cycle of poverty
Government Orders
for families. It takes so little in the way of programs that are geared toward mothers and children living in poverty, training programs that help young people who started out with a disadvantage in life to have a better opportunity.
We do not want to see programs that simply perpetuate poverty, but programs that give people a basic living while they move toward independence and also to provide a basis of support to those who for one reason or another cannot be independent. There are thousands and thousands of them in Canadian society. We have a healthier, saner society when we look after those who cannot look after themselves.
CAP contributes to basic necessities a very minimal living for people who temporarily need the help of society. We have seen how inadequate it is. We have seen how it is not enough to afford decent housing and so we need special housing programs. It is not enough to afford basic food and so we have food banks and volunteers and churches overwhelmed by the demand for extra support services. There are children going to school sometimes too undernourished to be able to profit from education and so we have in-school lunch and breakfast programs.
We have the implications of cutting back the contribution to the basic necessities of life. The implications fall most heavily on children. Poor children are four times more likely to drop out of school. Is that what we need in Canada? Is that what we need, that large proportion of our young people never finishing school, never developing the abilities they have, never being able to establish a stable and progressive employment record because they do not have the basic tools to work in Canadian society, to be steadily and well employed and remunerated enough to raise their own families? I do not think that is what we are looking for.
Mr. Speaker, you have already heard read into the record the health problems of poor children. I can tell you what happens in the schools when poor children enter kindergarten. They are stigmatized from the first day they enter school because their hair is not as glossy, their skin is not as bright, their clothes are not as nice, their shoes are not as shiny. By the time they have been in kindergarten for three months, before they are even six years old, those children already feel like failures. That is what we do to children when we let them grow up in poverty. That is what this bill will do.

Government Orders
We deprive children of any hope. We deprive their mothers of any hope. We deprive their brothers and sisters of any hope, and we deprive our society of any claim to being civilized and humane.
I know that the government seems very anxious to get itself out of any responsibility for making this a stronger and better society. It seems to think that the private sector is somehow going to take care of all of that for us. I do not believe that. If that were true we would not need governments. We would not need volunteer organizations. We would not need people who are looking constantly for ways to make this a country of opportunity for all Canadians and especially for all the children of Canada.
There is only one taxpayer's pocket, and the government can pretend that it is saving money with a bill like this. I am shocked that I have not seen, as the Prime Minister promised during the 1984 election, a similar massive review of subsidies to government. I cannot tell you how many tens of millions of dollars I have seen just coming across my desk in the last week in press announcements of $1 million here, $10 million there or $15 million there to companies in this country. Nobody has ever suggested that we should start cutting back on some of that money from the government side of this House. No, it is always the poor, is it not? It is always the children, the elderly and the sick that this government thinks should carry the burden of its mismanagement of the debt and the deficit.
I hope, in the better off communities within the three provinces that this government has targeted, social programs are going to survive because there are many communities in Ontario, B.C. and Alberta that have the resources to put in and make up where the government is not fulfilling its responsibility. But other programs in those communities will suffer. Programs that make up the basic necessities of food, clothing and shelter for families, other programs that help them get off welfare, that help them get training, that provide the extra support services needed to make life decent and liveable while they are on public assistance, those are the programs that will suffer. The extra little bit for dental care, for furniture, when a stove breaks, for back-to-school clothes for the children, those are what will suffer because there is only one taxpayer.
Many of those families now in Canada that are unemployed and poor will have to pay through their property taxes for what this government refuses to pay through a much more equitable tax base that it has access to. The property tax does not differentiate about whether you happen to be temporarily unemployed, on pension, poor or not. It is not based on income so you do not necessarily pay according to your means. So more of the burden will fall on fewer Canadians who can afford it.
The government by other actions has made the need for such services even more significant through the cutting back of benefits and unemployment insurance, which hits again most toughly in these three provinces. What it is doing is forcing more people on to welfare. As it is forcing more people on to welfare it is pulling back its own support from those very social programs that help people through a tough time and help them get back on their feet.
The bottom line is that this bill hurts not only those in the provinces that it is directly targeted at-and it is no easier to be poor in Ontario, B.C., Alberta or anywhere else, in many ways it is harder-but it hits our whole commitment to sharing in this country. People from the Atlantic provinces have spoken on this bill because they know that when we abandon that generosity of spirit that says all Canadians are entitled to a decent start and a decent chance, a helping hand over a rough period in their lives, then we start abandoning those segments of our country where we have to provide a little extra help.
It is important to all of us that Atlantic Canada be part of our country, not just to the people who live there. We have to be prepared to make it possible for the people of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland to benefit fully from being part of Canada if we want to enjoy the benefits.
Sometimes that involves paying a price, and we in the Liberal Party recognize there is a price to being Canadian and we are willing to pay it. We resent very much that this government is abandoning our commitment as Canadians to one another.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague from Ottawa West on her usual fine job of presenting arguments in an organized fashion on behalf of Canadians and on behalf, particularly I think this morning, of Canadian children.
September 24, 1991

I just wanted to get a reaction to something we find so prevalent in the country today. We have seen it mentioned here this morning, I think, by everyone who has spoken in the House so far, and that is the cynicism that is out there in Canada today. One does not have to go looking for it, it is so obvious wherever one goes. It affects politicians at whatever political level they happen to be: municipal, provincial or federal.
I just wanted to get the hon. member's reaction to something which I think has happened within the last week. I think it has some bearing on what she is referring to here in her speech. This cynicism is out there. It is going to take the efforts of all of us. It is something like a disease that is creeping across the land. I think it is going to take the efforts of all of us to try and put any kind of a damper on it.
One aspect of this will affect the hon. member in particular. Almost on the eve of provincial elections being called in two provinces, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, we find this government announcing almost simultaneously, let us put it that way, that an organization which has been headquartered here in this province will be suddenly removed from Ontario and put in Saskatchewan where there is a provincial election coming up within the next five or six weeks.
At the same time something in the nature of a science centre, I guess one could call it-both of these projects are very worth while-was announced. Another project would be put in, dropped in, placed in B.C., and an election was called there.
This is a double-barrelled example of the purest form of cynicism that exists in this country. Surely the Canadian viewing audience can see through the political moves that are afoot there and see it with straight cynicism. If Canadians are becoming more and more cynical, surely this feeds right into the hands of the cynics, and I think is gnawing at the very heart of the nation.
I wonder if my hon. friend from Ottawa West would just comment on that. I know one of those particular things is very near and dear to her.

I thank my colleague. Certainly we are well aware of and under-

stand the cynicism that is growing because we have seen a lack of trust in the government and a well deserved lack of trust. We have proclamations about the sacred trust of our social programs and yet we have-and it is not the first-a bill that is a very denial and destruction of the social programs that were being referred to.
Before every election this government referred to introducing a child care program. Three times it has reneged on that promise. We have seen money cuts to job creation, cutting opportunities for young people. We have seen the slashing of the registered home ownership savings plan so young people cannot afford their first home now. We have seen a surtax that was supposed to disappear when the GST came in. It has gone from 3 per cent up to 5 per cent instead of coming off. We saw Katimavik that gave new opportunities to our young people cancelled. We saw promises about not touching old age security. It was a sacred trust: "On the name and on the word and on the head of my mother I would not touch old age security". Whammo, six months later old age security and family allowances start being reduced and cut. Personal income tax has gone up. Those who are doing well in our society have more disposable income. Those who are poor have less disposable income, and now the feet are being cut out from under them again.
Yes, Canadians see themselves being bribed by then-own government to vote the way their government wants not only in federal elections. Oh, no, now they are down there interfering in provincial elections, trying to save Grant Devine's skin. Canadians see themselves being bribed by their own government to vote the way it wants, not only in federal elections, but now they are interfering in provincial elections, trying to save Grant Devine's skin from the negative effects he has created by moving Regina jobs out into rural Saskatchewan. They are moving federal jobs in to fill in the gap he has left, therefore disrupting two sets of families to achieve no positive results.

Mr. Speaker, I join with my colleague, the member who just spoke, in questioning the member who made the speech, in saying how much I enjoyed the remarks made by the member for Ottawa Centre.

Government Orders
There was some reference to the way poverty affects school children and I was wondering if the hon. member would perhaps take a more positive role and share with this House some of her ideas on the possibilities not only of cutting back on the moneys that are going in but perhaps inaugurating and instituting a program for younger children, school-aged kids, to be supplied with the basic fundamentals of life. I am talking very basically about at least a nutritious breakfast or something like that for those people who cannot afford it.
This problem is particularly acute in the larger cities, but not only there, and I am aware from my own background of having taught in schools that the problem does exist.
If the hon. member for Ottawa West would perhaps give us her views on that I would be most appreciative.

I thank my colleague for the question. That is exactly the kind of program that local communities can introduce for their children if they have the resources to do it and if they are not being required to meet the federal government's obligations to meet basic necessities of life through welfare systems.
I think it is even more important to back off a step before that. The successful programs I have seen involved very young mothers before their children were of school age, working with them around their own selfworth and the importance of their role as mothers in raising the next generation so that their children do develop a sense of pride and self-respect, that the mothers learn some skills that perhaps they did not learn growing up in their own families, so that the community as a whole is working to help mothers and their young children develop a new sense of pride, get the training they need, and get out of the welfare system.
In my view, the first thing is the community supporting the role of the mother with her child so that the sense of self-worth comes from within.

Mr. Speaker, I and my colleague voted against Bill C-69 when it was introduced in this House and we will be voting against Bill C-32 at third reading for a lot of reasons. One of the main reasons for opposing these two bills is that we believe
they in fact mark the beginning of the end of universal social programs as we know them in Canada.
According to many of the people who do research in the area and from all of the indications we received, by the year 2004, transfer payments to the provinces from the federal government in the areas of education and health care will be zero. There will be no transfer payments from the federal government to the provinces by the year 2004 in the areas of health care and education.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians know that when the federal government is not investing in the areas of education and health care it will not have the kind of say it wants to have in these two areas.
It surprises me somewhat that in the last budget the Prime Minister spoke very eloquently on the issue of education. He spoke about the question of objectives in the area of education. It was a very welcome statement at the time, but when one looks at the actions of the government in terms of Bill C-32 and before it, Bill C-69, one would question the commitment of the federal government to the educational question as well as to the health care question.
The whole issue is centred around reducing the deficit. There are three options which the government can take. One is to shut down operations and keep the taxes rolling for a few years. That will generate enough money and to pay the deficit.
Another option before the government is to do as it is doing now, reduce the services it is providing Canadians to a bare minimum and to attack many of the social health care programs, the social programs, that are veiy much needed in different parts of the country. It can sell national institutions such as Petro-Canada, Air Canada, VIA Rail and possibly CBC, et cetera, collect all this money and put it towards deficit reduction.
It can shut down a lot of the operations that are in place. We will still have a somewhat limping government, a somewhat half operational government, but we will still have a government and we will reduce the deficit.
September 24, 1991

There is a third alternative and that is the Liberal alternative, the Liberal way of reducing the deficit and revitalizing the economy in the country as a whole and that is through investment. We do not look at the question of putting money in the area of health care and education as being an expenditure, we look at it as being an investment in the future of Canadians.
The Minister of Finance and the Department of Finance in May 1990 said, when they spoke about the CAP spending restraint, that $147 million would be saved in the year 1990-91 and $154 million in 1991-92. The government at the time estimated that for the next five years it would be saving approximately $2.35 billion in transfer payments to Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario. Then the Minister of Finance of the province of Ontario, Mr. Nixon, estimated that would cost the province about $150 million in 1990-91 and approximately $280 million in 1991-92. The latest estimate which came a year later clearly stated that the loss to the province of Ontario would be approximately $1 billion in one year.
As a result of this move, the total share of social services which are provided by our regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton will be reduced tremendously. In fact, the Social Planning Council of Ottawa-Carleton predicts that the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan will cut revenues by $596 million over two years in the Ottawa-Carleton region alone. That is a tremendous amount of money, considering the increase in the social welfare payroll on an annual basis in this region is at least 10 per cent every year.
When the federal government cut the transfer payments to the provinces, the provinces in turn cut their transfer payments to the municipalities, and the municipalities find themselves trying to pick and choose, as my colleague from Ottawa West indicated, whether to increase the property taxes or let the people go hungry.
This downloading is creating a generation of people on the welfare market. In many cases they are not receiving the kind of care they deserve because of lack of funding. On the other hand, the government both at the federal level and at the provincial level are just shifting the problem without trying to address it with some sort of strategic plan.

Mr. Speaker, we must look at the impact of Bill C-32 on medicare and post-secondary education. Back in 1976, we had an agreement between the federal government and the provinces which stated that funding for post-secondary education was on a fifty-fifty basis. However, in 1986 the federal government started cutting the transfer payments to post-secondary education by 2 per cent every year, until the famous Bill C-69 arrived, which froze completely the transfer payments for 1990-91 and 1992 to the rate of inflation. From there it started going downhill.
These cuts in transfer payments have affected the delivery of services and programs at universities and colleges. For instance, the 1987-88 budget in the province of Quebec published a table which showed that the federal government would no longer put any money into medicare in Quebec by the year 2004, as I indicated earlier. That was with only the 2 per cent reduction in the federal funding formula which is presently being used. However, by 1990-91 the reduction would climb to 3 per cent and all the contributions would be frozen again for two years. All cash payments to all provinces, even the poorest, and that includes Atlantic Canada, will end some time around the turn of the century. Payment to Quebec will end by the year 1995 and in Ontario in 1998.
So as we are saying, less and less federal money for medicare and colleges and universities will put more of a financial burden squarely on the shoulders of the provinces. As a result, the federal government's ability to influence national standards and guidelines will be, as I indicated earlier, diminished.
When a survey was done across the country, 85 per cent of Canadians believed that medicare is our best and most valuable service.
When we look at the question of education, nobody could have put it any better than Jane Arnold, who is the chairman of the Canadian Federation of Students, when she said that education is a right and not a privilege. Bill C-69 and Bill C-32 take away the right and make education a privilege. Truly, Mr. Speaker, it will make education a privilege because, according to some statistics which were published in 1986, the higher education our children and our youth receive, the better chances they will have in receiving an education. The lower

September 24, 1991
Government Orders
education our youth receive, the less chances they will have in receiving an education.
Mr. Speaker, at a time when we have to put our emphasis on investment in our children and our youth, it is somewhat disappointing that the federal government is moving toward cutting many of the social and education programs that in fact would help in getting the country out of the difficulties we are in. There is no better investment the government can make than investing in our youth. There is no better way in dealing with reducing the level of deficit in Canada than investing in our youth.
Bill C-69 and Bill C-32 will be causing a lot of damage to the way we provide and offer our social programs across the country. Unfortunately CAP was the only remaining open-ended program that was cost shared between the provinces and the federal government. There was no limit on how much a province could choose to spend on some of the social services they are offering. The only limit they had is the fifty-fifty sharing agreement.
Mr. Speaker, when you look at the fact that approximately 40 per cent of the people who get welfare payments are children, research shows that poor children tend to have more health problems, greater difficulties in school and more involvement in crime than other children, and the cap on CAP makes sure that Canada does even less than in the past to combat these problems.
According to Dr. Robin Walker, president of the Canadian Council on Children and Youth: "About 40 per cent of social assistance recipients are children. The recent cap on CAP means that there will be less money to meet the basic needs of these children, to help their parents escape the welfare roles or to combat the negative effects of child poverty". He is absolutely right.
In fact, the situation is even more difficult when we look at the approximately 60 per cent of Indians living off-reserve in Canada who receive social assistance. A disproportionately large number of native children living off-reserve are cared for within British Columbia's child welfare system. We can conclude that aboriginal people in Canada represent one of the largest groups affected by restrictions on the amount of CAP transfer payments to the provinces.
Christopher McCormick, national spokesman on native issues for the Native Council of Canada, indicated: "Cuts to the Canada Assistance Plan will be a national disaster for aboriginal people who already live in Third World conditions".
On this subject matter one could speak on and on forever. The bottom line is that it is really up to this government to decide what it really wants to do. Does it want to invest in the future of Canadians now, or does it want to shut down operations and go home?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment on Bill C-32. First, I would like to congratulate my colleague, the member for Ottawa Centre, who has just put so well and so correctly all the damage this bill will cause.
I too of course am against this Bill C-32 because it will result in cuts to the provinces. We already know how badly the province of Ontario is mismanaged by the present New Democratic government that is there. Take that and add to it the cuts in transfer payments and we are in for some major difficulty. My fear is that these cuts to the provinces will result in our inability to train our population because a great Canadian once said the following about our ability to compete as a nation, Mr. Speaker, and I ask you to pay close attention to this. He said:
First, we require co-operation to re-establish the concept of working together as Canadians first. The concept around which this nation was built.
Second, we must make an effort to ensure that we have the capital required to finance national development in the 1980s, including a commitment from all sides to avoid the kind of vexatious and punitive policies that serve only to drive away Canadian foreign capital.
Third, we need a major national program to train and retrain the richest resource of all, our people, so that all Canadians may share in our development by working and by paying our own way.
Who was that enlightened person?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: I am glad my colleagues just asked me who that great Canadian was, because I just quoted from the book Where I Stand written by one Brian Mulroney.
That must have been a long time ago.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for his comments. I think the statement made in the book is a true statement. There is a lot of merit to it. I think the challenge of the government is in fact to do the delivery that would match what is in the statement.
September 24, 1991
